Prologue

I wasn't always this person.

There have been so many versions of me, each one shaped by a different phase of life. Some phases went gracefully. Some took the rugged path. Plenty came with mistakes I had to learn from.

I think of it like clay on a sculptor's wheel. What starts as a shapeless lump slowly becomes something detailed and precise, one patient touch at a time. I'm still on the wheel. With the right guidance, I'm trusting the process.

The name Aaquila

From the Arabic root ʿ-Q-L, tied to reason and understanding. It means wise, or intelligent. My parents chose it. I'm still learning to live up to it.

رَبِّ زِدْنِي عِلْمًا · My Lord, increase me in knowledge

Mamma, you are the one who began this story.
Until we meet again.

Part one

The story so far

01HomeKerala, India

I grew up where the monsoon is loud and everything grows.

Kerala, in the south of India, is home. At school and in college, I said yes to almost everything. I designed outfits for our fashion team, made decorations and pookalam (the flower carpets we make for Onam, Kerala's harvest festival), drew kolam (patterns drawn on the ground with rice flour), ran relays, did long jump and shot put, recited poems, gave speeches, and made bookmarks and posters for competitions.

In college I was elected house captain. I got to lead our house through the big events while joining in myself: group dance, fashion shows, a short film, elocution. And I played volleyball, as captain, every chance I got.

Being a captain shaped me more than any subject did. I learned that leading means looking out for people: helping each person find where they shine, and being the calm one when things get loud. Deadlines clashed, rehearsals ran late and nerves ran high, and somewhere in all that pressure I learned to enjoy it and still get it done.

We're only able to do something because we were given the chance to. So I try to be grateful, enjoy what I do, and make the best of it.

None of it was about collecting prizes. It taught me two things I still use every day: notice the small details, and break a big task into small steps you can actually do. One step at a time, even the hardest thing gets done.

fashion designdecorationflower carpets (pookalam)rice-flour art (kolam)relaylong jumpshot putrecitationelocutionposter makinggroup danceshort filmvolleyball
02Learning how things workRajagiri, Kochi · 2018 to 2022

I wanted to know what was inside everything.

I studied Applied Electronics and Instrumentation at Rajagiri School of Engineering and Technology. I loved the moments where theory turned into something you could hold: measuring, sensing, controlling.

My first real project came straight from the volleyball court. Line Touch Technology was a line-calling aid that could tell when a player's body landed on the centre line, then signal the referee with an LED and a beep. Later, our team built a quadcopter and used ArduPilot's Mission Planner to fly it on its own, carrying a payload along a set path.

That drone taught me something I didn't expect. Building the thing is only half of it. The other half is making it useful to the people it's for.

03Two pathsCOVID · 2020 to 2021

When the world shut its doors, we knocked on them.

I grew up around business as much as engineering, and for a long time I thought I had to choose one. Then COVID arrived. The people in nearby apartments couldn't get out, and our family farm still had fruit, eggs and fresh produce. So I took it to their doors, and online. Then mango season came. Then I started baking cakes.

I didn't know how to run a business. I tried, fixed what didn't work, and kept going. Somewhere in there I realised I don't have to pick between the engineer and the businesswoman. They help each other.

04First steps into workIndia · 2022 to 2023

Learning how real work works.

After graduating, I joined Kovenantz Technologies as a project management trainee, making Power BI dashboards and sitting in on sprint planning. Then I worked on a round-the-clock helpdesk at DXC Technology for an international client. Nights, weekends, and people who needed help right now. It taught me patience, and that a clear handover note is a kindness to whoever comes next.

05Crossing the oceanMelbourne · 2023

I crossed an ocean to see how big the world really is.

In 2023, I came to Australia to study my master's, for the exposure and the chance to learn as much as I could. In Melbourne I coached and refereed volleyball at two clubs and worked the Christmas rush at ALDI's warehouse. Refereeing taught me to make a call, explain it clearly, and stay calm when people disagree.

06Everything brokeResearch, Kochi · 2023 to 2024

Everything broke. That was the best part.

Back in Kochi, I joined a government-funded research team building a hardware accelerator to spot unusual activity in CCTV footage. Everyone around me was a PhD scholar or an experienced engineer, and I had never touched an FPGA. For the first week, I felt completely out of place.

So I gave myself one hour each morning to learn one small thing. Slowly, the conversations started making sense. Then I got my own task: connect a camera to a Zynq 7000 board. I went from shop to shop to find a module that matched the board. My first code gave me nothing at all. I stopped guessing, tested one piece at a time, and in the end it worked.

A problem only feels impossible while it's still one big lump.

07A pause2024 to 2025

Some chapters you don't get to choose.

Then life called me home. My family needed me, so I stayed. It wasn't easy. But it taught me patience, and what really matters. In July 2025, I opened my books again, this time in Brisbane.

08Finding my fieldBrisbane · 2025 to now

The grid is changing, and I'd like to help it change well.

At the University of Queensland, I found the part of electrical engineering I enjoy most. Electricity markets and how they actually operate. Transmission and distribution, and how power gets from a generator to a kettle. Research, where you get to ask questions nobody has quite answered yet.

My thesis is one piece of that: how much rooftop solar a street can safely send back into the grid. It's a big part of this year, but it's not the whole of me. I still enjoy the electronics and signals side too, and I've found I love presenting. Give me a room and something to explain, and I'm happy.

09Things I makeAlways

If it's in my head, I want to hold it in my hands.

I enjoy designing and creating new things, and turning ideas into something real. Right now that's websites, including this one, and a small clothing brand I'm building with my family. I'd always rather try something than give up on it before it starts. I do my best to make it happen, and if it doesn't work the first time, I learn and try again.

And then there's food. I'm always cooking something new, or baking cookies and brownies. My code is usually less buggy than my baking. Usually.

Interlude

Me, on a normal day

Outgoing, but I like my own quiet too.

I love being around people: talking, playing games, exploring food together. I also need my own space to think, and that's usually where my ideas show up. I enjoy both. And I love working in a team, and with the team: we talk it through together, then go and get it done.

Give me water and I'll swim. Give me a quiet spot outdoors and I'll stop and watch: the colours, the light, the little creatures going about their day. Nature is the most beautiful thing I know, and I love trying to catch it with a camera.

I speak English, Hindi, Malayalam and Tamil. My family is spread across Australia, India and the UAE, and spending time with them is my favourite thing.

What the chapters taught me

How I work

  1. 1

    Make it smaller

    A big task becomes a list of small, doable steps. Then I start on the first one.

  2. 2

    Notice the details

    From pookalam to power-flow results, the small things are usually where it goes right or wrong.

  3. 3

    Test one piece at a time

    When something breaks, I stop guessing and rule things out one by one.

  4. 4

    Ask, then listen

    I'd rather ask the simple question early. And if you tell me what to fix, I'll fix it.

I can promise I'll give it my best, and when I need to improve, I'll listen, learn and do it better.

Appendix A · Master's thesis · UQ · 2026

Learning dynamic operating envelopes from imperfect data

How much solar can each house push back into the street before the voltage goes too high?

On a sunny afternoon, rooftop solar can push street voltages up until inverters switch off. Networks are moving from a fixed export cap to dynamic operating envelopes: limits for each house that change through the day.

The accurate way to set them is optimal power flow, which needs a correct model of every cable. Real networks rarely have one. So my question is: can a learned model still set safe limits when the network data it's given is wrong?

253 VThe voltage at which rooftop inverters must disconnect under AS/NZS 4777.2.
4 wiresI model all three phases and the neutral, because on unbalanced streets the neutral matters.
1 errorCable impedance error, chosen with my supervisors and studied in depth rather than many errors studied thinly.

What I've built so far

  1. A four-wire optimal power flow benchmark in Julia, cross-checked against OpenDSS so the two tools agree before I trust either.
  2. A clean labelled dataset of safe export limits on a 55-customer feeder model.
  3. A realistic error model for cable data: a cable that isn't exactly as labelled (scatter), or the wrong cable type on record (bias).
  4. One firm rule: the optimiser always sees the true network, so the labels stay honest. Only the learner's view gets the errors.

What it's taught me

  • “Converged” doesn't mean correct.A simulation said it had solved, but every voltage was zero. Now my scripts check the answer, not just the status.
  • Say exactly what you measured.Phase-to-ground and phase-to-neutral voltages told different stories on my feeder. I report which one, every time.
  • Chase the mismatch.When a baseline didn't match my earlier seminar, I traced both numbers back to their source instead of picking one.

Supervised by Prof. Archie Chapman and Prof. Frederik Geth · Julia, JuMP, Ipopt, OpenDSS · Submitting November 2026

Grid frequency with more renewables

What happens to frequency when spinning generators are replaced by inverters?

PSSEPythonUQ 2026
−1.11 Hzdeepest dip, 2 inverter units
  • Automated three PSSE dynamic cases with Python, swapping synchronous generators for inverter-based units one at a time.
  • The same disturbance pulled frequency lower each time: 49.47 Hz, then 49.20 Hz, then 48.89 Hz.
  • Less spinning inertia means a faster, deeper fall. That's why grid-forming inverters and fast frequency response matter.
